1.d4 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and controls e4 without committing a central pawn, so White cannot easily build a full pawn centre. Black lets White occupy the centre and plans to undermine it from a distance with pieces and pawn breaks. The cost is that Black claims nothing in the centre yet.

1.d4 d5.strategy: Occupies the centre and stops e4, which White can now play only as a gambit. It mirrors White's set-up and tends to lead to positional, often closed play in which the pawn structure matters more than tactics. The cost is flexibility: with the d-pawn committed, Black must be ready to defend it against pressure from c4.

1.d4 e6.strategy: Opens the diagonal of the dark-squared bishop and leaves Black's plans open, since the game can still become French-like, Queen's Gambit-like or Indian in character. The price is the light-squared bishop, which stays behind the e6 pawn, and that White may claim the centre with e4 at once.

1.d4 f5.strategy: Stakes a claim to e4 and aims for an attack on White's kingside, with unbalanced, fighting play. The price is a weakened kingside, above all the e8-h5 diagonal, which White can test early with pawn sacrifices or a quick kingside pawn storm.

1.d4 Nc6.name: Bogoljubov–Mikenas Defence
1.d4 Nc6.background: Named after Efim Bogoljubov and Vladas Mikėnas. Hypermodern players such as Aron Nimzowitsch and Bogoljubov tried 1...Nc6, but it has never become very popular.
1.d4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a knight towards the centre and prepares ...e5, but blocks the c-pawn, which Black would normally keep free until White's set-up is clear. 2.d5 gains space and chases the knight away, usually to e5. Sound enough, but rare and committal.

1.d4 b6.name: English Defence
1.d4 b6.background: The English Defence is characterised by 1.d4 e6 2.c4 b6, but it can also arise from 1.d4 b6, especially at club level, where some players adopt 1...b6 and 2...Bb7 as a universal system. It was taken up in the 1970s by leading English players such as Tony Miles and Raymond Keene, and Viktor Korchnoi used it successfully in game 6 of his Candidates semi-final against Lev Polugaevsky at Évian 1977.
1.d4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 to pressure e4 along the long diagonal. Black lets White build a broad centre and means to undermine it with pieces instead of occupying it. Sound but rare, and Black has to play accurately against the space White gains.

1.d4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a solid pawn chain behind it and keeps the light-squared bishop free. Sound, but Black commits the c-pawn early, and White decides what kind of game follows.

1.d4 c5.name: Old Benoni Defence
1.d4 c5.background: The Benoni name goes back to Aaron Reinganum's 1825 book Ben-Oni, which besides defences to the King's and Queen's Gambits analysed the then unknown 1.d4 c5. The line is sometimes called the Blackburne Defence after Joseph Henry Blackburne, the first player known to have used it successfully. It has never attracted serious interest in high-level play, though Alexander Alekhine beat Efim Bogoljubov with it in one game of their second match, in 1934.
1.d4 c5.strategy: Attacks d4 at once and challenges the centre from the side. White usually gains space with 2.d5, and that advantage lasts while Black looks for counterplay against the advanced pawn. Playable, but Black starts a step behind in space.

1.d4 d6.name: Pillsbury Defence
1.d4 d6.strategy: Prepares ...Nf6 and a flexible set-up. Sound but modest: it develops nothing, and White gains space and chooses the line it prefers.

1.d4 g6.name: Modern Defence
1.d4 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 and lets White build a centre, to be attacked later by the g7 bishop and pawn breaks such as ...c5 or ...e5. Sound, but White gets a broad pawn centre before Black's pieces can challenge it.

1.d4 Na6.name: Australian Defence
1.d4 Na6.strategy: Develops the knight to the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but does little for the centre. White simply takes space while the knight still needs several moves to become useful.

1.d4 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where 2.Bxh6 gxh6 leaves Black with doubled, isolated h-pawns and a damaged kingside for only the bishop pair. Even without the exchange the knight does little for the centre.

1.d4 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rook-pawn move that prepares ...b5 but neither develops a piece nor contests the centre. White builds a full centre at leisure.

1.d4 a5.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rook-pawn move that controls b4 but does nothing for the centre or development. White is free to build a broad centre.

1.d4 b5.name: Polish Defence
1.d4 b5.background: Named by analogy with the Polish Opening, 1.b4. Alexander Wagner played 1.d4 b5 against Kuhn in the 1913 Swiss Correspondence Championship and published an analysis in Deutsches Wochenschach in 1914, and Boris Spassky played it against Tigran Petrosian in game 22 of their 1966 World Championship match.
1.d4 b5.strategy: Gains queenside space but neglects the centre and leaves the b5-pawn loose: after 2.e4 the bishop on f1 aims at b5, and defending or recovering the pawn costs Black time.

1.d4 e5.name: Englund Gambit
1.d4 e5.background: Named after the Swedish player Fritz Englund (1871–1933), who sponsored a thematic tournament in 1932–33 in which every game began with the position after 4.Qd5. Kārlis Bētiņš (1867–1943) introduced the main line with 2...Nc6 and 3...Qe7, and Henry Charlick, the second Australian champion, introduced the 2...d6 line in the early 1890s.
1.d4 e5.strategy: Offers the e-pawn for quick development and trap chances, such as a queen raid on the b2-pawn. Accurate play lets White keep the pawn or a clear lead, so the compensation is questionable.

1.d4 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the knight, weakens e6 and the e8-h5 diagonal, and develops nothing. After 2.e4 White has a broad centre and ideas of Qh5+.

1.d4 h6.strategy: Stops Bg5 but spends a tempo on a rook-pawn move that neither develops a piece nor contests the centre. White is free to take space.

1.d4 h5.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rook-pawn advance that develops nothing, ignores the centre and weakens g6. White is free to take the centre.

1.d4 g5.name: Borg Defence: Borg Gambit
1.d4 g5.strategy: Hangs the g-pawn to 2.Bxg5 and weakens the whole kingside. Even with the bishop on the long diagonal it only eyes d4, which White easily defends, and White stays a clean pawn up.

1.d4.name: Queen's Pawn Game
1.d4.background: Unusual in the 19th century, when 1.e4 was by far the most common move. Its merits were explored in the 20th, first through the Queen's Gambit, then through the Indian defences the hypermoderns popularised.
